heading: A city built from scratch
body: Chandigarh doesn't have ancient temples or medieval forts on its map, and that absence is the point: it is India's only major city that was designed and built, from a blank site, after independence — and its history is genuinely a 20th-century one, not a modern gloss on an old settlement. When Partition in 1947 cut Punjab in two and left its historic capital, Lahore, on the Pakistani side, the Indian half of the state needed a new one. In 1948 the government chose a stretch of agricultural land below the Shivalik hills, and in 1949 the American architect Albert Mayer was commissioned to plan a garden city there. Mayer withdrew after his collaborator died in a plane crash, and in 1951 the commission passed to the Swiss-French modernist Le Corbusier, who reworked Mayer's plan into a strict grid of numbered, self-contained sectors and designed the monumental Capitol Complex — the High Court, Secretariat and Legislative Assembly — in his signature raw concrete.

Building the city meant displacing roughly 21,000 people from 58 villages that stood on the site, a cost the planning histories record but that tourism-facing accounts often skip. Construction ran through the 1950s, with most of the city substantially complete by the early 1960s, and Chandigarh went on to serve a second unusual role: it is the joint capital of two separate states, Punjab and Haryana, while itself being governed as a Union Territory directly by New Delhi. The Capitol Complex was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016, one of very few 20th-century architectural sites on that list.

The map's Chandigarh entries are accordingly about planning and architecture rather than dynasties or battles — Le Corbusier's sectors, the Capitol Complex, and the design experiment that grew out of Partition's redrawing of Punjab.
